name: Tho-Radia radium cream

lead: Tho-Radia was a French beauty brand launched in 1932-1933 by pharmacist Alexis Moussalli and physician Alfred Curie. Its cream, powders and soaps were advertised as restoring a fresh, glowing complexion and firmer-looking skin.

The pitch drew on "microcurietherapy", the 1910s idea that tiny radium doses could stimulate living cells. Early creams were reported to contain radium bromide and thorium chloride; later products were described as thorium-only. The brand ran until 1968.

paras: It was sold as a face cream and a range of related cosmetics (powder, toothpaste, soap) in pharmacies and through heavy advertising, including radio sponsorship. Women applied it as an ordinary complexion product.

The products contained radioactive elements, and radium and thorium are hazardous. French rules from 1937 limited radioactive materials to medical prescription with poison labelling, after which the brand re-registered without mentioning radium. The product is historical and no longer sold.

angle.text: Tho-Radia was sold to women as a complexion cream that would revive the skin and give it a youthful glow. The promise rested on the then-popular microcurietherapy idea rather than on controlled studies.

lead: Tho-Radia was a French cosmetics brand sold between 1932 and 1968 whose best-known product, a face cream, was advertised as a way to keep the complexion fresh and youthful-looking by means of radium and thorium.[1] It was created by the pharmacist Alexis Moussalli, who worked at the Millot laboratories in Paris, together with Dr Alfred Curie, a physician unrelated to Pierre and Marie Curie whose surname served as a marketing asset.[1]

The brand was launched in Paris in 1932 and nationally in 1933 and drew on "microcurietherapy", an idea from the 1910s that very small doses of radiation could stimulate cells.[1][2] Historians of pharmacy have traced the product from its roots near the Institut Pasteur to its Radio Luxembourg advertising.[3] Tho-Radia is one of several radium cosmetics sold in the interwar years.[4]

paras: Alfred Curie registered the Tho-Radia brand on 29 November 1932.[1] The French-American company SECOR marketed it. A July 1932 analysis reportedly found about 0.223 microgram of radium bromide per 100 grams of cream.[1] Advertising by the illustrator Tony Burnand showed a young blonde woman lit from below by rays, an image used into the 1950s.[1]

In 1937 French rules restricted radioactive materials to medical prescription and required a red poison or toxic label; on 23 April 1937 SECOR re-registered the brand without referring to radium or Alfred Curie.[1] Later powder, toothpaste and soap were described as containing only thorium.[1] During the Second World War the firm relocated from Paris to Vichy, and business recovered from 1948 with perfume and lipstick.[1] After Moussalli died in 1955 the brand lost market share; it was sold to Lafarge in 1962, its Vichy factory closed in 1965 and the brand was abandoned in 1968.[1]

Microcurietherapy held that minute radium doses stimulate living cells. Wikipedia notes these notions were never scientifically demonstrated.[1] Radium was also sold in the period as a general tonic and in other cosmetic brands such as Artes, Ramey and Radior.[4]

Radium and thorium are radioactive; the best-documented radium harms in the period were among dial painters, who developed anemia, bone fractures and jaw necrosis.[4] Restrictions on consumer radioactive products in France began in 1937.[1]
No studies found. The Tho-Radia cream has been examined only in historical articles on its origins and commercial history.[2][3]
